fixes.answer: I do not think it is strictly necessary, though it certainly helps in many fields. A degree provides knowledge, [[credentials]] and valuable connections, and for professions like medicine it is essential. However, success can absolutely be achieved through other routes, such as vocational training or [[entrepreneurship]]. In my view, a degree is a powerful tool, but it is not the only path, and it is no [[guarantee]] of success.

I believe both are equally valuable, just for different purposes, and society needs both. Academic education develops theoretical knowledge and critical thinking, suited to research and the professions. Vocational training provides practical, [[job-ready]] skills that are in high demand and often lead directly to employment. Unfortunately, vocational paths are often unfairly [[stigmatised]], when in reality [[skilled trades]] are absolutely essential and highly rewarding.
fixes.why: 'essential' and 'rewarding' are plain; marked 'job-ready' and 'skilled trades'

fixes.answer: There are several reasons. Firstly, a degree is often seen as a minimum requirement for many good jobs, so there is [[mounting pressure]] to obtain one. There is also considerable social [[prestige]] attached to a university education in many cultures. Additionally, university offers young people independence and a chance to grow. However, this rush has led to some [[devaluation]] of degrees, as they become more common.
fixes.why: 'pressure' is plain and repeated in topic; changed to 'mounting pressure'

fixes.answer: I expect universities to become more flexible and accessible. Online and hybrid degrees will likely become [[mainstream]], allowing people to study while working. There may be a shift towards shorter, more [[modular]] courses focused on specific skills rather than lengthy traditional degrees. Universities will also need to work more closely with industry to ensure their qualifications remain relevant in a [[fast-changing]] economy.

This is a [[pressing issue]] in many countries. Governments could increase funding and [[subsidies]] to keep public universities affordable, treating education as an investment rather than a cost. Expanding scholarships and income-based repayment schemes would help ensure that talent, not wealth, determines access. Promoting quality alternatives, like online courses and apprenticeships, would also [[relieve pressure]] on the traditional, expensive model.
fixes.why: 'access' and 'model' are plain; marked 'pressing issue', 'subsidies', 'relieve pressure'

fixes.answer: There is some truth to this in certain fields. The rapid expansion of higher education has, in some cases, led to a [[surplus]] of graduates in particular subjects, resulting in [[underemployment]] and a [[mismatch]] with the job market. However, I would not say education itself is the problem. The real issue is the lack of alignment between what people study and what the economy actually demands.
